newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK economic strategist sees market turmoil by 2000.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK economic strategist sees market turmoil by 2000.

text.p: William Houston, British author of a series of books warning business folk about the ominously cyclical behaviour of history, climate and markets, is predicting a global collapse of bond and stock markets between now and the start of the 21st century.

Houston, a 68-year-old former weapons officer in the British Navy, turned lecturer and company doctor, publishes his predictions and their consequences in his latest book "Through the Whirlwind -Strategies for Survival" this week.

"It would only take one (G7 country) default for government bond markets round the world to dry up...no investor would trust the bond market, also making it extremely difficult for the stock markets to hold up," he told Reuters.

"This is the history of cycles -- we're going to see problems like earthquakes and disease piling up in the next century. Investors should also look at the 1929 (the Wall Street crash) parallels," he added.

Houston is part of an honourable, if somewhat eccentric, tradition of economic forecasting going back at least to the mid-19th century which traces a raft of metereological, disease, economic and historical cycles spanning scores of decades or even one which recurs every 500 years.

A board member of the Foundation for the Study of Cycles -- putting him in the upper echelons of cycle gurus, he has written for national newspapers, using historical parallels to anticipate contemporary crises, highlighting in one case the resemblance between Britain's Henry VIII's break with Rome in the 1500s and the likely consequences in the 1990s of Britain rejecting full European union.
KONDRATIEFF AND HIS THEORY OF THE 45-60 YEAR ECONOMIC CYCLE

According to Houston, cycle adherents agree the most influential cycle in recent times is the Kondratieff 45-60 year 'long wave' named after its originator, a Russian economist studying in Moscow in the 1920s.

Studying historic interest rates, commodity and finished goods prices in Britain, the United States and France, the Russian concluded economies at various times have moved in distinct phases -- the upwave, a period of expansion out of recession; an in-between phase called the plateau stage; and the downwave marking the return to recession. Kondratieff forsaw the deep depression in the 1930s using his observations. The state later sent him to Siberia for his pains.

Now in the late 1990s, Houston says, "a highly singular confluence of important cycles (including the Kondratieff long wave) are reaching their low point." Other possible contributors to turmoil include a cycle which produces major upsets every 500 years and one which triggers climatic and historical changes during a 179-year drought cycle.

Houston sees contemporary financial markets riding an economic downwave which started in 1990, the symptoms of which include recession, rising real interest rates, a collapse of credit and mounting national debts.
COUNTDOWN TO DEBT MARKET MELTDOWN
The last of these -- crippling debts -- may prove the final straw for markets, says Houston.

"Corporate and public institutions' debts are reckoned currently to be running at $20 trillion compared with world GDP of some $25 trillion, which puts leverage at about 80 percent. But this doesn't take account of about $50 trillion in off-balance sheet or derivative debts," Houston said.

The debt mountain will weigh ever more heavily on bond markets. Houston believes the one-off failure of an indebted Western country like Italy or Sweden to service its loans, or even a natural disaster -- a huge earthquake centred in Tokyo for example -- could trigger a fatal collapse in capital markets.

"A Tokyo quake, part of a 70-year cycle in rising seismic activity, would affect some five percent of the world's GDP. There would be a huge sucking noise of securities being repatriated to pay for what could amount to $5.0 trillion in damages," he said.

Moreover, says Houston, unless countries start paying back debt -- a move almost all except New Zealand are loath to initiate -- a default among the indebted G7-type countries is now a distinct possibility. More so when the downwave of an economic cycle means that governments will find it harder to raise cash from hard-pushed taxpayers to repay loans, Houston notes.

"Should this (a default) happen then major insurance and pension fund holders would be progressively reluctant to hold bonds and instead would buy sound equities on the principle that companies are more likely to protect their solvency than governments."

In this 'doomsday' scenario, governments would struggle to sell bonds to investors and would have either to raise taxes or cut spending to balance budgets. Failing this, they could print more money to pay their debts, unleashing the sort of rampant inflation seen in Germany in the 1930s.
Also any rise in the price of wheat -- prompted in the next few years by the return of cool, dry climates -- would fan the flames of inflation and mete out further damage to bonds.
"The best investments would be food processing, mining, precious metals or energy stocks and probably gold," he said.
STOCK MARKETS TO TEETER, GOVERNMENTS' POWER ERODED
While stocks could remain a good alternative in the short-term, Houston is convinced equity markets would falter in the face of crumbling bond markets.
"The yield on the S&P and the Dow (the leading U.S. blue-chip indices) are less than two percent, the highest it's ever been, making it very vulnerable to a downturn.
"Now a number of economists believe that the strong dollar will also reduce the capacity of U.S. corporations to increase their earnings to justify that low yield," Houston said.

The implications for governments if stock and bond markets collapse, as Houston forsees it, may include a gradual reduction in their influence over individuals as the state runs out of funds to keep afloat centralised services such as education, welfare and healthcare.

"We are probably near the end of the need for centralised government which is associated with the Industrial Revolution. You are going to get communities taking matters into their own hands," he said.

Investors wanting to finance pensions may shun enfeebled public markets and invest instead in local businesses. As Houston sees it, the brave new 21st century will usher in a period of individualism and financial experimentation: "What's the point of centralised markets if they can be at the whim not only of cycles but of cynical politicians and central banks?"
